Chapter 1: Rethinking Success—Applying Business Theories to Life’s Big Questions
Let me ask you—have you ever found yourself caught up in chasing promotions, bigger paychecks, or impressive titles, without really stopping to think about what actually brings you joy? It’s easy to get swept away by those traditional ideas of achievement. But what if I told you the same business models companies use to thrive could help you shape a more meaningful personal life?
Here’s the first step: challenge those default definitions of success. True fulfillment doesn’t just show up because you’ve got status or wealth—it comes from making conscious choices that line up with your values.
Think about how businesses operate. They’re always weighing strategy models, figuring out where to invest for the best long-term results. Why not do the same for your own life? What if you paused and asked yourself, “What does a good life really look like for me? What matters most—and am I actually spending my days on those things?”
Imagine your life as a portfolio of investments. Just like a company decides where to put its capital, you can choose where to put your time and energy. Is it going toward activities and relationships that truly matter to you? Every so often, it’s worth checking in—are your current pursuits leading you closer to the life you want, or are you just reacting to what the world expects?
Now, there’s a trap almost everyone falls into at some point—the “achievement trap.” That’s when you chase after things that are easy to measure, like salary or job title, but overlook the stuff that actually makes you happy: growing as a person, deep connections, a sense of purpose. In business, it’s like chasing quick profits and ignoring the company’s long-term health. Remember, what gets measured gets managed—but not everything that matters can be measured.
So, how do you avoid drifting away from what’s truly important? Here are a few things to keep in mind:
First, define success for yourself based on your values and sense of purpose—not just on what the outside world rewards. Next, take time now and then to reflect. Are your daily choices moving you closer to those values, or further away? And finally, recognize that fulfillment isn’t a box you check once—it’s an ongoing process, something you build over time.
Adopting this approach—treating life’s big choices as strategic decisions—lays the foundation for real, lasting satisfaction. When you start using business thinking to navigate your own journey, you can create a life that feels genuinely meaningful, not just impressive on paper.
